title: Walking-Talking Mock Exams: 5 ways to make them effective
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton examines the common Walking-Talking Mock, where a year group copies a teacher's projected solutions onto blank exam papers, and argues that the sound core idea of hearing an expert think aloud is undermined by five problems. Students are not cognitively active, the teacher gets no data, everyone is fooled that learning is happening, strong students gain little, and the annotated paper is hard to revise from. For each problem he pairs a fix: try each question first with confidence scores, gather answers on mini-whiteboards, check understanding with a follow-up question, stretch secure students with What if questions, and have students build quizzable Review Cards from their highest-confidence errors. The move is to keep the format but restore retrieval, assessment and revision value, with a candid caveat that his experience is limited to maths.
points: Having students attempt each question before the explanation, with a confidence score, keeps them thinking and sets up the Hypercorrection Effect.
Mini-whiteboard checks give the teacher data, with about 80 percent correct suggested as a benchmark for moving on, so time goes to questions students actually struggle with.
A silent room of nodders is a poor proxy for understanding, so explanations should be followed by a same-difficulty follow-up question that cannot be solved by swapping a number.
What if questions stretch students who already have a question secure, and can lead a struggling student to succeed at harder variations.
Review Cards built from the highest-confidence errors give students a quizzable revision system, which beats re-reading annotated corrections.
quotes: Students dutifully copy down said solutions on their copy of the exam paper. Other teachers patrol the room to keep an eye on behaviour and help students out if needed.

Just because nobody asks any questions doesn’t mean anybody understands. And students may be tricked into thinking they understand as they happily copy down the teacher’s work - ah yes, that’s what I would have written!
We know from research that re-reading is an inferior learning strategy to practice-testing, but the problem with notes in an exam paper is that it makes it very hard to do anything but re-read.

This can be further improved by asking students to indicate their confidence in each of their answers - I use a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 indicates the student knows their answer is wrong, and 10 indicates they are sure they have nailed it.

If the mini-whiteboard check reveals understanding is not as secure as we would like - everyone will have their benchmark for this, but 80% correct is a good target to aim for - then we can ask students to lower their boards, empty their hands, and listen as we carefully talk through the solution, sharing our thinking for each step of working.
This should test the same context, and be of the same difficulty, but also require some thinking - students should not be able to simply swap a number around and have the answer.
The inherent problem with corrections is that they are unquizzable. It is challenging for students to revise from their corrections to a Walking-Talking mock effectively.
